## From Prediction to Action {#sec-boundary-prediction-to-action}

The acting line begins with feedback. Wiener's cybernetics described animals and machines alike as systems that measure the result of their own action and use it to correct the next one [@wiener1948cybernetics], and control theory soon learned to estimate a moving system's state from noisy measurements [@kalman1960new]. The first industrial robots needed little of this at the level of the task. In 1961 a Unimate arm began stacking hot die-cast parts at General Motors by replaying step-by-step commands stored on a magnetic drum [@chm1961unimate]. Nothing in that program could notice a person in the arm's path, so protecting people meant keeping them out of its reach. The machine acted, but it did not perceive, and nothing in it was learned. The two lines this section follows, robotics and control learning to act and machine learning mastering prediction, run as the upper and lower lanes of @fig-01-evolution until they merge.

title: Three machine classes
caption: **Three machine classes**: Each class is named for the constraint that dominates it and the margin it spends: (a) mass-dominated mobility (Class 1) spends stopping clearance, set by momentum and braking; (b) contact-dominated manipulation (Class 2) spends force and deformation margin, set by contact stiffness and the strength of the object and mechanism; and (c) energy- and thermal-dominated operation (Class 3) spends heat and supply margin, set by Joule heating, thermal capacitance, and power delivery.
alt: Three panels. Class 1, mass-dominated mobility: a wheeled base moving at speed v toward a rack end, with the clear distance D clear marked in red, above the relation d stop equals v tau delay plus v squared over 2 a brake. Class 2, contact-dominated manipulation: an arm whose gripper presses a spring of stiffness k contact into a stiff fixture, deformation delta x and force F in red, above F approximately equals k contact delta x. Class 3, energy- and thermal-dominated: power P in entering a winding of thermal capacitance C th, heat P out leaving, and a temperature bar T wind below a red T limit line, above d T wind over d t equals P in minus P out over C th. Each panel names the margin it spends: stopping clearance, force and deformation margin, heat and supply margin.
context:
**Contact-dominated manipulation** (Class 2) spends force and deformation margin. When an articulated arm presses against a stiff fixture, minute position displacements can generate destructive contact forces over fractions of a millimeter. Physical contact is both the means of task success (seating a part or opening a latch requires deliberate force) and the immediate hazard. The engineering task is to supply the wrenches (the combined forces and torques) needed to complete the assembly while guaranteeing that contact forces never exceed the mechanical yield limits of the payload or the manipulator.

**Energy- and thermal-dominated operation** (Class 3) spends heat and electrical supply margins. Supporting a heavy load or resisting gravity demands sustained motor current, driving continuous Joule heating in actuator windings even when joints remain stationary. Concurrent peak current draws from drive inverters, compute accelerators, and sensor payloads can induce voltage sag across a shared DC bus. The system must sustain these thermal and electrical loads across the entire operational profile while reserving sufficient energy and thermal headroom to execute a safe protective abort.

title: The physical AI scope test
caption: **The physical AI scope test**: Physical AI combines a learned component, consequential physical feedback, and delegated authority to let learned outputs reach actuation without human approval. An independent veto belongs inside this intersection because accepted proposals can still move the plant. The pairwise overlaps locate advisory systems, digital autonomy, and classical control.
alt: Three-set Venn diagram defining physical AI at the intersection of learned models, physical feedback, and delegated authority. The pairwise overlaps show advisory systems, digital autonomy, and classical control.
context:
Together, these three criteria delineate the domain of physical AI. The three-set Venn diagram in @fig-01-scope-venn formalizes this boundary, locating physical AI at the central intersection where a learned model, consequential physical feedback, and delegated authority converge. Each pairwise overlap holds systems that meet only two of the three criteria. Advisory systems place a learned model inside a physical process, as when a technician inspects learned toolpaths before loading them onto a mill, but a person still approves each action. Digital autonomy executes learned outputs without human approval, as in an automated trading engine, but its actions land in software rather than in physics. Classical control closes a physical feedback loop automatically, as in a PID speed governor, but relies on an analytical control law rather than a learned model. Excluding these pairwise overlaps restricts the design problem to systems where statistical uncertainty collides directly with physical irreversibility.

[^fn-sysid-scope-test]: **System Identification**: The control-engineering practice of fitting low-order dynamic models to measured input-output time series. When this fitting establishes bounded parameter uncertainty under stated modeling assumptions, control engineers can use those bounds to prove stability guarantees before deploying the controller. Modern high-dimensional neural networks lack tractable closed-form uncertainty bounds and therefore require empirical verification across explicitly specified operating domains. \index{System identification!scope test}

On a March night in 2018, a modified Volvo XC90 operating Uber Advanced Technologies Group's developmental automated driving system (ADS) struck and fatally injured a pedestrian pushing a bicycle across a road in Tempe, Arizona [@ntsb2019uber].[^fn-inc-tempe-investigation] The vehicle carried a roof-mounted lidar, forward and side radars, surround cameras, and GPS antennas, all routed to ADS compute and data-storage racks in the cargo bay (@fig-01-tempe-vehicle). Reading each time as an interval before impact, rather than as a clock time, is what lets it be converted into distance traveled at the recorded speed, the conversion this section applies.

context:
system of records illustrated in @fig-01-spine formalizes this progression, capturing operating assumptions and empirical evidence so that downstream runtime decisions can inspect and rely on them. Conceptually, these records trace two converging pipelines. One strand establishes offline physical limits and verified competence; the second processes online sensor observations and real-time candidate actions. Both pipelines converge at the permission decision, where the system admits or rejects a proposed trajectory. In @sec-frontier-architectural-synthesis, this architecture synthesizes both strands to resolve the book's central challenge of engineering dependable, high-performance physical systems out of unverified learned models and unforgiving mechanical hardware.

A record is a machine-checkable artifact that downstream safety and runtime decisions can verify and trust. The initial stopping calculation (notebook \ref{nbk-boundary-stopping-budget}) already sketches the first record in the chain: a limit record, with the six elements the reader guide introduces (nominal value, operating conditions, uncertainty, margin, runtime detector, and provenance). Its nominal value is the derived stopping distance under stated operating conditions of loaded payload mass, dry concrete, a stationary obstacle, and constant approach speed. Because those inputs are illustrative scalars rather than calibrated distributions, however, its uncertainty remains unquantified. The apparent buffer between the obstacle and the machine is therefore only an arithmetic difference between provisional figures rather than a verified safety margin. The calculation also lacks a runtime detector—no sensor yet monitors whether floor traction drops or cargo shifts outside the assumed envelope (@sec-body-limit-record-schema)—and its provenance rests on baseline assumptions rather than calibrated hardware logs. An ungrounded calculation becomes operational engineering evidence only when all six fields are populated and backed by empirical data. Every numbered box across the four part bands in @fig-01-spine establishes a machine-checkable record of this rigor for a distinct architectural decision.

title: Strain wave gear set
caption: **Strain wave gear set**: The three parts of a Harmonic Drive strain wave gear, disassembled: the elliptical wave generator with its thin-race ball bearing (top left), the flexspline cup with external teeth on its open rim (top right), and the rigid circular spline ring with internal teeth (bottom). The wave generator bends the flexspline so that its teeth mesh with the circular spline at two opposite zones; because the flexspline carries slightly fewer teeth, each turn of the wave generator advances it by only that difference, which gives a high reduction with little backlash. (Credit: Pieceofmetalwork, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.)
alt: Photograph of three machined steel parts on a white surface: a round ball bearing assembly at top left, a cylindrical cup with fine teeth around its rim at top right, and a flat ring with fine internal teeth and bolt holes at the bottom.

context:
[^fn-strain-wave-origin]: **Strain Wave Gearing**\index{Strain wave gearing!origin}: @musser1959strain patented the mechanism, now sold as the Harmonic Drive: an elliptical wave generator flexes a thin toothed cup inside a rigid ring that carries two more teeth, so a single stage yields a high ratio with near-zero backlash. The flexing that makes the ratio possible is also the joint's torsional compliance, which makes the link elastic.

[^fn-limit-cycle-backlash]: **Limit Cycle**\index{Limit cycle!backlash}: A self-sustained oscillation of fixed amplitude that a nonlinear feedback loop settles into, here excited by the backlash deadband as the motor crosses the gap, the teeth strike, and the controller corrects back across it. Unlike an instability, it does not grow, so it can run unnoticed through a shift while every cycle adds a tooth impact to the fatigue count.

The strain wave gear of @fig-02-real-strain-wave-gear packs a high reduction into a compact joint by deforming its flexspline continuously, and that elasticity has a cost. This intentional compliance decouples rotor position from link position under dynamic loading: while the motor encoder registers smooth rotation, the flexspline winds up like a torsion spring, introducing unmeasured end-effector deflection.

title: Motor stator damaged by overheating
caption: **Motor stator damaged by overheating**: The opened stator of an electric motor that failed from overheating, showing the copper phase windings bound with tape at left, the insulating slot liners where the windings leave the laminated iron core, and the end bell with its bearing seat at right. The windings are where resistive heat ($\WindingLossPower = \TorqueProducingCurrent^2 \EffectiveLossResistance$) is generated, and the insulation between them is what accumulated heat ages. (Credit: K. Kudelina, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0.)
alt: Color photograph looking into an opened electric motor stator: dark copper wire windings bound with fabric tape on the left, pale insulation paper protruding from slots in a laminated steel core that recedes toward the right, and a round end bell with a bearing seat at the far right.
context:
Reducing motor current to shed heat also reduces holding torque. A loaded arm therefore needs a response that preserves support, such as transferring the load to a mechanical brake, rather than assuming that thermal derating leaves the task unchanged. Excess winding temperature can damage electrical insulation, while excess rotor temperature can permanently reduce magnet strength. Those material limits bound the allowable temperature trajectory.

The winding and housing respond on different timescales. Copper heats rapidly under current, while the larger core and housing absorb and reject heat more slowly. A case temperature measurement can therefore lag the winding hotspot during a torque burst. The stator in @fig-02-real-burnt-motor-stator failed from overheating, and its damage sits where this model puts the heat: in the copper windings and the insulation between them.

The burst calculation limits duration, while the back-EMF relation in @sec-body-electrical-time-constants limits torque at speed. A feasible maneuver must satisfy both. At low speed, the drive can supply the current needed for a burst, but the winding temperature limits how long it may do so. At higher speed, back-EMF consumes voltage headroom and can prevent that current from appearing at all. On the arm's stand-in joint motor, voltage headroom and thermal history bound the usable torque-speed region simultaneously (@fig-02-motor-torque-speed-envelope). context:
A learned proposer earns its place in an embodied system when training distribution coverage generalizes beyond preprogrammed edge cases. In the conveyor pick task, this capability translates into interpreting natural language instructions, recognizing the target mug amid visual clutter, and proposing reachable grasp affordances. However, high-level semantic identification alone cannot direct a robot arm; the system must project proposed grasp regions into metric Cartesian space using calibrated depth sensing and forward kinematics. Furthermore, environmental challenges such as specular reflections, dynamic shadows, and transient occlusions inevitably induce perceptual errors. Whatever algorithmic sophistication a proposer introduces, its execution demands must conform to the throughput, memory bandwidth, and thermal dissipation envelope of the onboard processor.

A first estimate shows why one model cannot do both jobs. If every fresh evaluation must stream all of a model's weights from off-chip memory, its renewal rate can be no higher than the sustained bandwidth divided by the bytes of weights, a ceiling that falls in proportion to parameter count (@fig-cadence-gap). The intent model stores its weights as 4-bit integers (INT4, priced in @sec-brain-quantization) rather than 16-bit floating point (FP16), which raises its ceiling fourfold. Both of the machine's proposers still sit below their ceilings, because reading the input tokens in one pass through the model (the *prefill*) and then decoding the output add work that weight streaming alone ignores. Neither approaches the kilohertz rate at which the permission path and the servo loops run. The design problem is therefore deciding which computation can finish before the observation it started from goes stale. @Sec-brain-memory-wall derives the ceiling and the work above it; the figure is a preview of where the derivation lands.

In a bimanual teleoperation workcell (@fig-aloha-manipulator), an operator moves low-cost leader arms while follower arms with parallel grippers reproduce the motion, and overhead and wrist cameras record what the followers saw. Those recordings become the training data for policies that later act alone [@zhao2023learning; @chi2024diffusionpolicy]. The running machine's chunk policy takes its size from ACT, which was trained on exactly such recordings. What such a policy learns from them is the action chunk itself, a short stretch of the operator's motion predicted from one view. How demonstrations become a policy belongs to @sec-training; this chapter prices what the trained policy costs to run. Although learned representations tolerate sensory variations captured across training distributions, executing any proposed motion safely still demands calibrated spatial geometry and strict physical boundary enforcement. Empirical task success demonstrates capability over tested operating envelopes, but out-of-distribution shifts in illumination, surface friction, or payload dynamics can quickly induce behavioral drift or outright failure.

The computational cost of this capability depends directly on the model's underlying representation. A transformer does not read pixels or words directly; it reads *tokens*\index{Token!embedding of an input slice}, embedding vectors that each represent one slice of input, such as an image patch, a word fragment, or a joint angle. Across a VLA model, that token sequence flows from camera patches and prompt embeddings through self-attention to candidate action chunks (@fig-vla-architecture). Multi-view camera frames consume significant memory bandwidth during ingestion, historical context expands key-value (KV) cache footprints in memory, and the inference engine must produce subsequent actions before the physical state diverges from the initial observation. Evaluating an embodied learned model alongside a classical perception-planning pipeline requires assessing both task generalization and the end-to-end latency required to refresh action proposals.

caption: **Illustrative embodied roofline**: Arithmetic intensity (operations per byte moved from off-chip memory, @eq-brain-arithmetic-intensity) against attainable throughput using the application processor's dense FP16 GPU ceiling and rounded peak memory bandwidth. Single-token weight streaming sits deep in the memory-bound region, while the intent model's prefill, which reuses each fetched weight across all of its input tokens, lies past the ridge, the intensity at which the bandwidth roof meets the compute roof, where compute binds. context:
For the dense weight projections of single-token decoding at batch size 1, each a matrix-vector product $\LayerOutputVector = \WeightMatrix\LayerInputVector$, counting weight traffic alone gives an optimistic estimate, because activation and context traffic add further bytes. In FP16 each weight occupies 2 bytes and participates in exactly one multiply-accumulate operation (2 FLOPs), so
$$\HalfPrecisionGemvIntensity = \frac{2\,\text{FLOPs}}{2\,\text{Bytes}} = 1.0\,\text{FLOP/byte}$$
The roofline model [@williams2009roofline] turns that ratio into a bound (@fig-patterson-roofline). It plots attainable throughput against arithmetic intensity as two roofs. Below a crossover, the ridge point, throughput is capped by a sloped roof equal to bandwidth times the intensity; above it, by a flat roof equal to the processor's peak arithmetic rate. It is read the same way as the stopping-budget plot of @sec-boundary-kinematic-roofline, where delay travel and braking travel trade dominance at a crossover speed. Both plots show two regimes and the point at which one gives way to the other.

The fastest loop sits beside its sensor and its switch, so phase current is measured and switched next to the winding with no host processor in the loop. Dedicated PWM timers in the same silicon enforce the gap between complementary switch transitions that keeps the power bridge from shorting.[^fn-hw-epwm-deadtime] The running machine's brushless hub drives follow this arrangement at a larger scale; the small stepper-motor driver of @fig-real-motor-controller shows it on one chip.

Actuator commands also demand strict temporal freshness. Even when delivered comfortably within a deterministic transport window, a setpoint computed from stale perception is functionally hazardous. The evidence timestamp and lease expiry embedded in the command proposal remain safeguards even over nanosecond-synchronized fieldbuses. The transport budget must reserve adequate headroom for physical actuation to execute, and the real-time permission path must reject any setpoint whose authoritative validity window has expired.

[^fn-net-tsn-fieldbus]: **Time-Sensitive Networking**\index{Time-sensitive networking}: IEEE 802.1Qbv Time-Sensitive Networking provides bounded Ethernet delivery by configuring time-aware traffic shapers across network switches. High-priority control frames travel inside dedicated, pre-scheduled transmission windows, while asynchronous high-bandwidth traffic (such as uncompressed camera streams) is held back at the switch gates. This scheduled time-division multiplexing lets camera streams and microsecond servo commands share a physical link without packet collisions or switch-queue buildup.

context:
## Actuation Authority {#sec-nervous-actuation-authority}

A shared mailbox cannot protect a mobile manipulator if the host processor retains a diagnostic route, an auxiliary bus master, or a JTAG debug port that writes directly to a drive. The silicon partition established in @sec-nervous-silicon-partitioning therefore requires exclusive physical control over every electrical path capable of energizing the motor windings. Actuation authority is this exclusive physical ability to modify drive states, encompassing PWM configuration registers, current references, gate-driver outputs, and bridge-enable lines. Under this architecture, the host publishes candidate proposals $\CandidateProposal_t$ and the safety microcontroller's permission path alone turns them into admitted commands $\AdmittedCommand_t$. The difference between holding that authority and merely appearing to is a question of wiring (@fig-04-privilege-enforcer-registers). When the permission path is the sole writer of the drive registers and can trip a drive inhibit, every motion passes its checks. When the host can also write those registers, one unchecked write reaches the motors, and proposer and drives share a single failure domain.

title: Illustrative out-of-band interlock and STO path
caption: **Illustrative out-of-band interlock and STO path**: Each emergency-stop contact holds its own force-guided relay, and each relay's enable contact holds one of the drive's two STO inputs, so a single welded contact or shorted wire leaves the other channel able to remove torque. The EDM contacts report a relay that failed to release before restart. Removing torque leaves the motor free to coast; the spring-applied brake is a separate circuit that clamps when its supply is removed. The diagram shows a hardware response path, not a certified integrity level or a stopping distance (synthesized from ISO 13849-1 and IEC 61800-5-2).
alt: Two-channel schematic. A red positive-break E-stop is mechanically linked to two normally closed contacts, S1 and S2, each fed from 24 volts. S1 feeds the coil of force-guided relay K1 and S2 the coil of relay K2; each relay has a normally open enable contact and a normally closed EDM contact. K1 sends STO1 enable and K2 sends STO2 enable to two STO terminals on the drive, which feed the gate-drive supply and then the inverter bridge driving motor M. A red tag above the motor reads tau equals 0, and a note below reads may coast. The two EDM contacts are wired in series with a dashed teal line to a reset monitor, restart only if K1 and K2 released. At the bottom, a brake supply on its own circuit, switched by K1 and K2, contacts not drawn, feeds a spring brake that clamps on power loss and acts on the motor shaft. A note reads hardware only, no processor in this path.
context:
If the safety microcontroller itself hangs or suffers a clock failure, it cannot execute a software-directed stop. A hardwired, out-of-band interlock must therefore supervise the system and enforce a qualified fallback state. Safe Torque Off (STO) accomplishes this by disabling gate-driver optocouplers or charge pumps through hardware logic, preventing the inverter from generating rotating magnetic fields.[^fn-std-iec61800-sto] STO does not isolate the high-voltage DC bus from the mains, nor does it guarantee that momentum will dissipate within the stopping clearance allocated for powered deceleration. Complete electrical isolation requires an upstream safety contactor, and containing gravitational drop or mechanical drift requires a certified electromechanical brake. A dual-channel interlock circuit (the relay network of @fig-real-estop) decouples torque inhibition entirely from the host software stack. Safety qualification must still verify that the system remains resilient against common-cause failures in power rails, clock crystals, and harness wiring.

[^fn-std-iec61800-sto]: **Safe Torque Off (STO)**\index{Safe torque off}: An STO implementation removes torque-producing drive signals through a hardware interlock. An IEC 61800-5-2 integrity rating depends on the actual devices, diagnostic coverage, wiring, and validation, not on the circuit pattern alone [@iec61800part52].

title: The latch corridor seen from above
caption: **The latch corridor seen from above**: Retained demonstrations supply dense forward-progress actions inside a narrow corridor centered on the strike plate. A gripper displaced toward the fixture sits where the archive holds no demonstration, so nothing in the data specifies the action that returns it to the corridor, and an unconstrained output can carry it farther toward contact.
alt: Top-view sketch. A shaded horizontal corridor runs left to right toward a strike plate on the right, with five arrows pointing along its centerline. Above the corridor, a small square marks a displaced gripper. A dashed arrow from the gripper toward the corridor is labeled as the missing return action, and a dashed arrow from the gripper toward a shaded fixture band at the top is labeled as drift into contact.
context:
Opening a latch from a nominal centered approach and recovering from an off-axis sideways slip require different physical actions (@fig-05-latch-corridor). Every retained demonstration guides the gripper forward along the narrow corridor centered on the strike plate, which populates the archive with thousands of forward-progress actions. The archive contains zero demonstrations that start from a gripper displaced a few millimeters toward the fixture and return it to the centerline. Because a skilled human operator rarely lets the gripper drift into those boundary regions, and because teleoperation runs that drifted noticeably were aborted or discarded during curation, nothing in the training data constrains the policy's output at such a displaced state.[^fn-alvinn-recovery-latch] The **recoverability problem**\index{Recoverability problem} is this absence of demonstrated corrective actions that steer the system back into the nominal corridor.

[^fn-alvinn-recovery-latch]: **ALVINN (Autonomous Land Vehicle in a Neural Network)**\index{ALVINN!recovery data}: Pomerleau's road-following network learned to steer from a human driver who kept the van centered, so its training images held almost no off-center views [@pomerleau1989alvinn]. His remedy shifted each camera image sideways in software and corrected the steering label to match, synthesizing recovery examples about 20 years before Dataset Aggregation (DAgger, @sec-data-intervention-recovery) [@pomerleau1991efficient]. A warp could fill that gap because the missing state was only a viewpoint of a flat road, whereas a gripper displaced toward the fixture also lacks contact forces that no image transform can manufacture, so its recoveries must be demonstrated or collected.

title: Four-stream action tap tuple
caption: **Four-stream action tap tuple**: Four places a command can be logged, from raw policy intent on the application processor through to measured plant response. Which tap a dataset records decides what the model learns to imitate. The four-tap decomposition is this book's construct; the teleoperation rigs it instruments follow @zhao2023learning and @wu2023gello.
alt: Block diagram. On the application processor, a policy or operator box feeds a kinematic mapping box; tap 1, a req, sits between them and tap 2, a cmd, sits after the mapping. A black-channel link with no shared memory crosses the dashed proposal boundary to the discrete safety MCU, which holds the permission path at a 1 kHz tick. Tap 3, a enf, sits after the permission path, which feeds the drives that close the current loops and apply the torque limit. The drives move the plant, joint encoders measure the motion over an interval, and tap 4, a meas, leaves the encoders. All four taps run down to a synchronized telemetry log stamped with hardware timestamps.
context:
### The four-stream action tap tuple {#sec-data-four-stream-action-tap}

If a dataset keeps only one signal from those two processing domains, any discrepancy between what the operator asked for and how the arm actually moved becomes impossible to diagnose. A command must therefore be logged at each of the four causal stages it passes through. The **four-stream action tap**\index{Four-stream action tap!definition}\index{Action tap!definition} $(\RequestedActionTap, \MappedCommandTap, \EnforcedCommandTap, \MeasuredResponseTap)$ records all four in one hardware-synchronized telemetry log (@fig-05-action-taps). Two are logged on the unprivileged Linux host before the black-channel link, and two on the discrete safety MCU after the 1 kHz permission check. Logged together, the taps keep interventions and tracking errors auditable.

title: One lag, three verdicts
caption: **One lag, three verdicts**: Pairing an observation with an action across an uncompensated lag displaces the recorded state by speed times lag. At `{python} SyncDisplacement.t_lag_str` the transit pairing is `{python} SyncDisplacement.dx_transit_str` off, the faster latch approach exceeds the `{python} SyncDisplacement.clearance_str` clearance, and the guarded approach stays inside it. The clearance tolerates at most `{python} SyncDisplacement.lag_max_fast_str` of lag at `{python} SyncDisplacement.v_fast_str` and `{python} SyncDisplacement.lag_max_guarded_str` at `{python} SyncDisplacement.v_guarded_str`; a full-frame rolling-shutter skew alone spans `{python} SyncDisplacement.t_skew_lo_str` to `{python} SyncDisplacement.t_skew_hi_str`.
alt: Log-log plot of pairing displacement in millimeters against observation-to-action lag in milliseconds, 1 to 100 ms. Three straight parallel lines: transit at 0.50 meters per second on top, the faster latch approach at 0.10 meters per second, and the guarded approach at 0.03 meters per second at the bottom. A red dashed horizontal line marks the 2 millimeter latch clearance. A dotted vertical line at 35 ms marks the uncompensated lag, with a dot on each line. Red squares where the latch lines cross the clearance are labeled at most 20 ms and at most 66.7 ms. A gray band from 15 to 33 ms marks full-frame rolling-shutter skew.
context:
:::

When an imitation learning model trains on misaligned pairs, it fits a relationship in which the action appears to precede the visual evidence that prompted it. During closed-loop deployment, that artificial phase lag appears as overshoot, control hunting, and chattering against rigid surfaces. Because displacement grows linearly with lag, each approach speed has a lag ceiling equal to the clearance divided by the speed, and @fig-05-sync-displacement places those ceilings beside a second timing error the notebook did not count. A rolling-shutter sensor exposes its pixel rows one after another rather than all at once, so the bottom row of a frame is captured later than the top (@sec-data-rolling-shutter-skew quantifies the delay). A full-frame rolling-shutter skew of `{python} SyncDisplacement.t_skew_lo_str` to `{python} SyncDisplacement.t_skew_hi_str` is comparable to the uncompensated lag, so a logger that stamps every frame correctly can still breach the faster approach's `{python} SyncDisplacement.lag_max_fast_str` ceiling through readout alone.

title: Kinematically isomorphic teleoperation loop
caption: **Kinematically isomorphic teleoperation loop**: The operator moves a leader arm whose joints mirror the follower's, and the host copies joint angles across, as in low-cost leader-follower rigs such as GELLO [@wu2023gello]. Because the leader shares the follower's joint structure, the interface needs no inverse kinematics and inherits none of its singularities (configurations where joints align and the arm loses a direction of motion), preserving the operator's direct joint-level coordination. The loop still closes through the operator: human reaction, command transfer, mechanical response, and display delay all enter the recording as phase lag, so the demonstration carries the operator's delay as if it were policy.
alt: Block diagram of a teleoperation loop. An operator box labeled see, decide, move sends an arrow labeled t hum to a small leader arm with joints q1, q2, and q3. The leader feeds a joint copy box stating q follower equals q leader, noted no inverse kinematics, which sends an arrow labeled t cmd to a larger follower arm with the same three joints, reaching toward a latch across a gap labeled t mech. A dashed arrow runs from the follower down to a workspace camera, whose arrow labeled t disp runs left to a display, which feeds back up to the operator.

Every retained episode approaches the strike plate at the guarded speed of `{python} LatchScenarioTable.v_guarded_str` with the plate aligned within ±`{python} LatchScenarioTable.logged_offset_str` of nominal, and every successful demonstration stays below the illustrative `{python} LatchScenarioTable.f_trip_str` detection threshold. title: Covariate shift and intervention curation
caption: **Covariate shift and intervention curation**: (a) The learned policy's own actions choose the states it sees next. The worst-case cost bound grows as $\CovariateDriftBound$ for behavioral cloning and as $\mathcal{O}(\DeviationDisadvantage\BehaviorCloningHorizon\AggregatedSurrogateLoss)$ for aggregation on a recoverable task; these are bound orders, not measured drift. (b) One takeover. The `{python} DataLookbackWindow.t_lookback_str` lookback reaches back past the divergence point; states between divergence and takeover are eligible for expert relabeling while the learner's commands there are masked. After takeover, the enforcer's blend and the operator's reorientation are retained for diagnosis but excluded from expert imitation targets, and only the reviewed segment from measured stabilization to recovery becomes an expert demonstration. Based on @ross2011reduction and @spencer2021feedback.

Right: tracking error against time, flat until t div and rising under the learner to a peak at t takeover. A dashed segment marks the enforcer blend, an oscillating segment marks the operator's reorientation, and from t stabilize the expert's curve falls smoothly to zero at t rec. A bracket marks a 5-second lookback window ending at t takeover and reaching back past t div. Below the axis, a row names the four intervals: drift, blend, re-orient, and stabilized. context:
A team can also avoid online interventions entirely, and this is the wide-tube remedy promised in @sec-data-curse-dimensionality-recoverability. Injecting small noise perturbations into the teleoperator's commands pushes the robot off the nominal path during ordinary collection, so the operator's corrections back toward the corridor appear in the initial demonstration set itself [@laskey2017dart]. Each perturbation consumes hardware life from the fatigue budget in @sec-data-yield-fatigue-budgeting and must stay within recoverable bounds. Ingestion pipelines therefore log the collection mode of every episode explicitly (nominal, noise-injected, or gated intervention), because the three modes put different kinds of states and labels into the archive.

[^fn-math-dagger-bound]: **Corrective Aggregation Error Bound**\index{DAgger!linear error bound}: The bound is Theorem 3.2 of @ross2011reduction. It holds for some policy in the sequence of $\AggregationRoundCount$ iterations, with $\AggregationRoundCount$ of order $\DeviationDisadvantage \BehaviorCloningHorizon$ up to logarithmic factors, and $\DeviationDisadvantage$ bounds the change in the expert's cost-to-go after any single action. @Sec-appendix-ml-compounding states the finite-sample form, in which the same constant appears as $\Glyph{u_{\max}}$.

section: Passive covariate shift vs. physical dynamics shift {#sec-data-passive-vs-physical-shift}
context:
calibration!planar target}: In practice $\CameraIntrinsicCalibrationMatrix$ is estimated from a few views of a planar checkerboard, the method @zhang2000flexible introduced, and the extrinsics come from a separate hand-eye calibration. Both describe one mounting at one time. The reprojection residual is therefore a calibration test repeated every session, not a setup step performed once.

@Fig-05-camera-calibration displays this verification pipeline across a $7 \times 7$ grid of workspace scenes from the DROID dataset. In each, a colored silhouette of the robot arm, rendered from its Unified Robot Description Format (URDF) kinematic mesh at the recorded joint angles, is projected through each camera's extrinsic calibration matrix and overlaid directly onto the raw photographic frame. Where the mask and the physical arm coincide, camera extrinsics and joint encoders are geometrically aligned; where the colored silhouette departs from the links, the check exposes camera mount slippage before corrupted trajectory pairs enter training. The DROID corpus showed how easily mount drift escapes standard checks. Although its cameras were initially calibrated with checkerboard targets during data collection, independent re-analysis revealed that rendered kinematic masks barely overlapped visible robot links across numerous recorded episodes [@lu2025ctrnetx]. The DROID research team subsequently evaluated stored extrinsics by measuring mask intersection-over-union, discarded failed sessions, re-estimated camera poses using learning-based hand-eye estimators, and published updated calibrations for approximately `{python} StateOfPractice.droid_recal_str` episodes [@khazatsky2024droid]. This calibration error shipped within a major open-source corpus because it was transparent to standard file format parsers. To prevent these silent failures, ingestion architectures must bind every recorded episode to an immutable calibration identifier and real-time clock synchronization metrics. Trajectories collected under conflicting geometric or temporal calibrations force neural policies to average incompatible sensorimotor distributions within identical state spaces.

title: Drift out of the demonstrated states
caption: **Drift out of the demonstrated states**: Behavioral cloning trains only inside the shaded tube the expert visited. Once the learner leaves it, each action is taken from an unfamiliar state and the error compounds. DAgger labels a learner-visited state outside the tube, which supplies recovery experience while a return is still possible. Past the red boundary, actuator and friction limits leave no action that restores the task, so no label can help. The sketch is schematic; its axes carry no units.
alt: Schematic state-space plot with task progress on the horizontal axis and deviation from the demonstrated path on the vertical axis. A shaded band surrounds a solid expert path. A dashed learner path leaves the band and continues upward into a red region at the top. At one point just outside the band, a marker labeled DAgger label has an arrow pointing back toward the band.
context:
:::

Expert availability also does not imply physical recoverability. The machine may lack enough actuator effort or frictional grip to return from a deviation. The simplified force balance $\GeneralizedInertiaMatrix\GeneralizedAccelerations = \JointTorque + \ExternalContactTorque$ is Newton's second law written per joint. Here $\GeneralizedCoordinates$ denotes joint positions, $\GeneralizedInertiaMatrix$ inertia, $\JointTorque$ actuator torque, and $\ExternalContactTorque$ the torque that contact forces exert about the joints. Other forces are omitted for clarity, and @sec-planning-rigidbody-dynamics develops the full equation. Actuator limits require $|\CommandedJointTorque_i| \le \JointTorqueLimit$ on every joint axis, while available friction bounds tangential force by $\|\TangentialContactShear\| \le \CoulombFrictionCoefficient \NormalContactForce$, with normal force $\NormalContactForce$ and friction coefficient $\CoulombFrictionCoefficient$. These constraints can leave no action that restores the task, and then $\DeviationDisadvantage$ is unbounded and DAgger's linear guarantee no longer applies. Interactive aggregation is therefore most useful where learner deviations can be contained, labeled, and repeated within the operator-time and hardware-exposure budget. The state space divides into three regions (@fig-06-compounding-error). Cloning trains in the tube of demonstrated states. Just outside it lies a band where an expert label on a learner-visited state still restores the task. Beyond the band is an unrecoverable region, where actuator and friction limits leave no restoring action and every further label is vacuous. Interactive aggregation buys experience only in the middle band.

title: Physical data-collection farm
caption: **Physical data-collection farm**: Between six and fourteen manipulators ran concurrently to collect over `{python} TrialWallClock.n_grasps_farm_str` grasp attempts over two months, using self-supervision to train an offline grasp-success predictor [@levine2018learning]. While hardware parallelism compresses calendar duration, aggregate system wear and operational costs continue to scale with the total trial count: each station adds capital depreciation, gearbox and bearing wear, motor winding thermal stress, and technician labor to clear dropped objects and mechanical jams. Attribution: @levine2018learning.
alt: Two stacked photographs of a row of white articulated robot arms on tables, one under daylight and one in a darkened room. Each arm has a two-finger gripper above a metal bin of household objects, with a camera on a post above and behind it.
context:
:::

Adding parallel rigs scales floor space, capital cost, electrical power infrastructure, and supervisory labor in direct proportion to $\ParallelRigCount$. A grasp-learning farm shows what that scale looks like (@fig-06-robot-arm-farm): up to `{python} TrialWallClock.n_rig_farm_str` arms, each with its own gripper, bin, and camera, ran day and night, and the cluster collected over `{python} TrialWallClock.n_grasps_farm_str` grasp attempts over two months. The farm was not running reinforcement learning. It used self-supervised grasp outcomes to train an offline success predictor, which an external servo loop queried to guide real-time grasping motions [@levine2018learning]. That is why it serves here as a picture of scale rather than of an algorithm. Whatever the learner, collecting close to $10^6$ physical trials takes a room of arms running for months and pays the wear that comes with it. section: The Simulator as a System Component {#sec-training-simulator-component}
context:
A reinforcement learning policy trained on door latching learned an aggressive, unbraked plunge because its simulated strike plate yielded far more than the physical mechanism. Stripping away the simulator during physical deployment does nothing to unlearn that behavior. The physics simulator is not an external sandbox; it is an active component of the training pipeline whose equations, contact approximations, and timing assumptions dictate the exact experience supplied to the optimizer. Accepting simulated task success as evidence of hardware readiness requires measurable, verifiable error bounds on every one of those assumptions.

Like any physical subsystem, a simulator requires a formal interface contract stated in quantities that engineers can measure and budget. This interface contract specifies observation dimensions, action bounds, simulation time step $\FiniteChange \TimeInstant$, transport latency between command issuance and physical actuation, actuator torque and current limits, sensor noise distributions, reset distributions, and termination conditions. For instance, if a simulator executes an observation loop at 100 Hz with an assumed zero-delay sensor channel and Gaussian noise of variance $\SensorNoiseStandardDeviation^2 = 1.0 \times 10^{-4}\text{ (rad/s)}^2$, the policy tunes its feedback gains to those exact signal statistics. An unmodeled 15 ms bus transport delay on the physical machine then removes $\CrossoverFrequency \PureTransportDelay$ of phase at the loop's crossover frequency $\CrossoverFrequency$ (@eq-nervous-delay-phase), and the loop goes unstable whenever that loss exceeds the phase margin the learned gains left. OpenAI's Dactyl project faced this contract at full scale, with a 24-DoF Shadow Hand in a motion-capture cage and its MuJoCo twin (@fig-06-sim2real-dactyl) [@andrychowicz2020learning]. The team calibrated the simulator against the physical hand and then randomized physical parameters around those calibrated values, so that the policy met the remaining discrepancies as variation it had already seen in training.

section: Teacher-student privileged state distillation and asymmetric actor-critic {#sec-training-privileged-distillation}
context:
Everything privileged stays on the simulation side, and only the frozen student's proposals, built from the machine's own sensor history and renewed every `{python} LatchContactDeadline.t_chunk_str`, cross to the permission path. In Phase 1, the privileged teacher policy $\pi_{\text{teacher}}(\CognitivePolicyAction_{t} \mid \PrivilegedSimulatorState, \MultimodalObservation_{t})$ learns an effective control strategy via standard reinforcement learning, exploiting full access to contact forces and surface friction. In Phase 2, the student policy $\pi_{\text{student}}(\CognitivePolicyAction_{t} \mid \ObservationHistoryWindow)$ is trained via supervised imitation learning (such as DAgger or behavioral cloning) to reproduce the teacher's proposed actions using only a sliding history of onboard observations. While this two-phase approach simplifies reinforcement learning exploration, it introduces a transfer bottleneck. If the teacher's control strategy relies on distinctions that cannot be reconstructed from the onboard observation history $\ObservationHistoryWindow$, the student cannot replicate the teacher's behavior. Privileged information accelerates training convergence, but it cannot make physically unobservable states identifiable on hardware.

Consider the cage-door latch mechanism. A student network equipped with a temporal history can compare commanded motor efforts against observed joint accelerations over recent timesteps, inferring changes in contact stiffness or friction through the resulting mechanical resistance. However, identical joint kinematics can arise from multiple distinct physical causes, and an unobserved geometric offset in the strike plate cannot be inferred simply because the simulation teacher possessed that knowledge. A temporal convolutional network or transformer encoder can output a learned latent embedding of the environment, but its accuracy must be audited against physical ground truth. Adding auxiliary loss functions to predict privileged parameters during distillation regularizes the representation, but an auxiliary loss cannot create physical information that is absent from the underlying sensor stream.

Minimizing loss on an offline demonstration split or maximizing cumulative return in simulation measures compliance with training assumptions rather than physical competence on hardware. When an objective rewards behavior that exploits a curated demonstration distribution or a simulator approximation, the ranking of candidates established in training can invert on deployment\index{Deployment!policy ranking inversion}. Virtual environments forgive maneuvers that physical hardware penalizes with tripwires, resonance, or thermal overload, so the causal assumptions connecting a training metric to physical execution have to be tested before a policy receives actuator authority.

context:
### The four evaluation evidence regimes {#sec-evaluation-four-regimes}

The first axis, causal feedback, governs whether a candidate's emitted actions alter future states and subsequent sensor observations ($\partial \MechanicalPlantState_{t+1}/\partial \CognitivePolicyAction_{t} \ne \ZeroVector$), or whether the policy merely reads a prerecorded, invariant sensory stream. In an open-loop configuration, execution errors cannot compound because mistakes never propagate into future inputs. In a closed loop, small policy errors perturb subsequent machine states and accumulate into compounding drift at a rate dictated by system dynamics and closed-loop feedback gains. The second axis, physical realism, governs whether sensory observations originate from physical transducers interacting with unmodeled contact dynamics, gear backlash, tire slip, and variable illumination ($\PhysicalPlantDynamics$), or instead emerge from a synthetic numerical simulator or static buffer ($\SimulatedPlantDynamics$). No single testing configuration can maximize both axes simultaneously without exposing expensive hardware, or nearby operators, to an unproven and potentially destructive policy. Each quadrant of @fig-07-evidence-regimes therefore provides evidence for specific claims and carries its own structural blind spot.

caption: **Standardized robotic evaluation facility**: NIST response-robot test bays photographed in 2013 (Linda Joy/NIST); their test methods are standardized by ASTM subcommittee E54.09 on response robots. context:
The door latch campaign shows why the contact shock entry in @tbl-07-extreme-value-tails pairs a measurement with an architectural safeguard rather than with a fitted tail. Each trial yields only one block maximum, its peak latch contact force, and twenty maxima cannot fit a generalized extreme value tail that would predict the probability of exceeding `{python} EvalMachine.f_latch_limit_str`. The guarded `{python} EvalMachine.v_approach_str` approach is a candidate precontact limit whose adequacy depends on the measured effective mass, contact stiffness, and structural threshold. Deploying parallel robots across a test fleet does not establish statistical independence, as the pitfall in definition \ref{dfn-evaluation-exposure-wall} warns. Ten identical machines operating concurrently in a single warehouse share the same manufacturing batch, firmware revision, concrete sealant finish, heating and ventilation airflow, and operator handling protocols. Environmental disturbances absent from that facility, such as low-angle winter solar glare, surface water pooling, or floor polishing glazing, affect none of the machines. Standardized physical test fixtures, such as the response-robot test bays captured in @fig-07-nist-test-arena, ensure repeatable benchmark comparisons by strictly constraining the test environment to known, fixed obstacle geometries.

section: Rolling shutter distortion and motion compensation
context:
Resolving this spatial artifact requires **rolling-shutter motion compensation**\index{Rolling-shutter motion compensation!definition}: unwarping image coordinates geometrically using an interpolated camera pose for every scanline. The onboard IMU supplies high-rate (`{python} RollingShutterSkew.f_imu_str`) angular velocity and specific-force[^fn-imu-specific-force] samples rather than direct velocity measurements. A fused state estimator integrates these inertial readings with bias estimates, gravity tracking, and wheel odometry to compute continuous body poses. Transforming these poses through calibrated body-to-camera extrinsics yields an estimated optical pose for each scanline, allowing the perception pipeline to rectify the image before running stereo matching or landmark triangulation. Plotted against row index, the uncompensated skew is a straight line, because each row is read a fixed interval after the one above it (@fig-08-rolling-shutter-rows). The line ends halfway to the `{python} RollingShutterSkew.delta_loc_str` allowance, which is why compensation, not a budget row, must absorb it.

[^fn-imu-specific-force]: **Specific Force**: An accelerometer measures non-gravitational acceleration, $\LinearAcceleration-\GravityVector$, so a unit resting on the floor reads one $\Gravity$ upward and one in free fall reads zero. Dead reckoning must therefore rotate specific force into the navigation frame and restore the gravity vector, and an attitude error $\AttitudeError$ leaks $\Gravity\sin\AttitudeError$ into horizontal acceleration, which integrates twice into the per-row poses that de-skewing relies on. \index{Inertial measurement unit!specific force}

A misdated measurement breaks this estimation algebra silently. Suppose a stereo depth observation is tagged with its host arrival timestamp, which @sec-perception-handoff shows hides exposure, readout, and transport delay, rather than with its physical exposure epoch. The filter erroneously pairs this observation with a robot pose `{python} AisleKalman.bias_misdate_str` further along the aisle than where the photons actually struck the sensor. context:
driven (@fig-09-odometry-drift), even the calibrated line crosses the bound only just past one `{python} OdometryDrift.aisle_length_str` aisle, which makes $\LocalizationBound$ a constraint on how often external map corrections arrive rather than an intrinsic property of the mobile base.

Three physical realities prevent this illustrative calibrated extrapolation from establishing an operational design margin. First, the laboratory benchmark operated at `{python} OdometryDrift.v_test_str` along straight segments to minimize wheel slip, stopping to pivot at each corner; production warehouse bases travel `{python} OdometryDrift.speed_ratio_mult_str` faster under varying operational payloads. Second, kinematic calibration eliminates only deterministic systematic errors. Non-systematic stochastic errors (floor irregularities and micro-slip) produced a run-to-run standard deviation of approximately `{python} OdometryDrift.sigma_run_str`, eclipsing the residual calibrated systematic error of `{python} OdometryDrift.e_cal_str`. Third, a constant per-meter error rate is merely a first-order linearization. An uncorrected heading error $\SmallChange\HeadingAngle$ produces lateral position displacement $\SmallChange\HeadingAngle\,\TraverseDistance$ over a straight traverse of distance $\TraverseDistance$. Because wheel-diameter mismatch causes heading error to accumulate linearly with distance ($\SmallChange\HeadingAngle \approx \HeadingCurvature \TraverseDistance$ for a constant heading curvature $\HeadingCurvature$), the resulting lateral error grows quadratically, about $\tfrac{1}{2}\HeadingCurvature \TraverseDistance^2$, quadrupling each time the straight run doubles. Under this illustrative drift model, reserving localization margin requires external corrections at intervals shorter than the calculated crossing distance; the deployed interval must come from the machine’s qualified drift envelope. In deployed systems, the site parameter $\LocalizationBound$ must be established empirically, by driving the robot past surveyed fiducials at nominal velocity and maximum payload across actual facility flooring, reporting drift rates at a defined operating percentile.

Supplying that identity is the job of semantic scene memory, which sits above the raw metric layer and inherits its physical constraints. Learned neural models infer what an object is, whereas the underlying metric mapping pipeline anchors where that object sits in physical space. Open-vocabulary scene memory bridges these domains using **3D vision foundation models**\index{3D vision foundation models}. A self-supervised visual backbone such as DINOv2 [@oquab2023dinov2] extracts dense patch feature representations. A promptable segmentation model such as the Segment Anything Model (SAM) [@kirillov2023segment] generates class-agnostic instance masks. Systems such as ConceptGraphs [@kuwajerwala2024conceptgraphs; @jatavallabhula2023conceptfusion] and Hydra [@hughes2022hydra] lift those 2D masks and semantic features through calibrated depth, extrinsics, and visual odometry into an **object-centric 3D scene graph**\index{Object-centric 3D scene graph!definition}. In this structured representation, each node represents an entity parameterized by a 3D centroid, a spatial covariance matrix, and a text-aligned multimodal embedding vector.

Drawn for the warehouse (@fig-09-dynamic-scene-graph), such a graph stacks five layers: a metric mesh, the objects and agents segmented from it (mugs, totes, the cage door, a walking person), topological places linked through free space, rooms such as aisles and dock bays, and the building itself. Edges between layers run both ways, compressing metric surfaces into symbols on the way up and grounding task tokens in metric coordinates on the way down.

Evaluating this bounded growth model with the scenario parameters yields `{python} LatchSlotBelief.growth_math`, where elapsed time $\FiniteChange \TimeInstant$ is in seconds and error $\BeliefErrorBound(\FiniteChange \TimeInstant)$ is in millimeters. Setting $\BeliefErrorBound(\FiniteChange \TimeInstant) = \PositionalTaskTolerance$ produces the quadratic characteristic equation `{python} LatchSlotBelief.quad_math`. The positive real root establishes an invalidation horizon of $\BeliefInvalidationHorizon =$ `{python} LatchSlotBelief.t_exp_str`. ## The Belief Record Schema {#sec-memory-spatial-state-schema}

The belief record introduced in @sec-memory-handoff, the seventh record in the record chain, binds each state estimate to its capture epoch, coordinate frame, and error-growth law so that downstream controllers can catch a frozen transform, a chimeric frame chain, or a prediction that has outlived its slot tolerance. This schema unifies discrete tracked entities and continuous volumetric representations (@tbl-09-schema-volumetric-belief) under one set of time and error rules, serving both trajectory planning on the host and bounded local permission checks on real-time microcontrollers. From the observation contracts established in @sec-perception-observation-contract, the record inherits the raw sensor capture epoch, clock identifier, and hardware conversion bound. For differently constrained state components, it preserves separate evidence epochs or a conservative shared epoch and growth bound, as required by @sec-memory-state-epoch. With these fields, the safety permission controller translates the sensor's capture timestamp into its own local monotonic clock with bounded synchronization error before evaluating evidence age. Persistent memory contributes five fields of its own. An estimate epoch dates the propagated state without renewing physical evidence. An uncertainty-growth bound projects error expansion across blind intervals. A validity region defines the operating envelope where that bound holds. The record also carries a physical invalidation deadline. Finally, a query-work allocation is set to at most `{python} RepresentationQuery.t_query_str` per local collision query in the reference design, and it becomes a justified execution bound only after qualification on the chosen hardware. Across its lifetime, each record moves through the four-state lifecycle of @fig-09-spatial-belief-state-machine, whose guards enforce two rules. Only fresh evidence returns a record to `VALID`, and leaving `UNOBSERVABLE` also requires restoring the missing physical constraint.

section: What each proposal family leaves to admission {#sec-intent-proposal-families}
context:
open-vocabulary phrase grounding from computer vision and natural language processing [@kamath2021mdetr; @gu2022open; @radford2021learning; @liu2023grounding], yet an embodied machine cannot rely on a model's internal activations for physical safety. For example, a semantic skill ranker like SayCan outputs a discrete skill identifier scored by language affordance and value functions [@ahn2022saycan]. A programmatic generator like Code as Policies produces a control script that calls perception and motion APIs [@liang2023code]. VoxPoser synthesizes 3D spatial value maps (@fig-10-value-map-composition). OK-Robot emits a distribution of sampled grasp poses (@fig-10-real-open-vocab-grounding). Because none of these outputs natively carries a bounded wrench envelope, a certified clearance margin, or a hardware lease expiration, choosing one model family over another only shifts where conversion happens and leaves the admission checks in @tbl-10-grounding-paradigms unchanged.

Predicting a syntactically valid coordinate or control script never guarantees physical feasibility. Vision-language and action models are trained to maximize sequence likelihood over offline demonstration datasets. Their loss functions encode neither metric distances, rigid-body collision avoidance, manipulator Jacobian conditioning, nor frictional contact dynamics. Validating a candidate action requires deterministic physical checks evaluated within explicit coordinate frames. These checks include signed-distance queries over robot and environment meshes to verify clearance, numerical inverse-kinematics solvers with joint-limit and singularity screening, and Coulomb friction models to confirm that the planned grasp wrench resists expected gravitational and inertial loads. For contact-rich tasks such as sliding an object, turning a latch, or executing a handover, the system can simulate candidate trajectories in a rigid-body physics engine before committing actuator current. However, simulation fidelity remains bounded by the accuracy of estimated surface friction and inertial parameters. Downstream controllers must still enforce real-time admission checks regardless of simulation outcomes.

section: The Intent Lease Specification and Contract {#sec-intent-lease}
context:
An intent lease progresses through five discrete lifecycle states on the Safety MCU: `Pending`, `Active`, `Renewed`, `Expired`, and `Aborted`. The controller transitions a proposal from `Pending` to `Active` only after verifying all geometric and dynamic ceilings and confirming that a collision-free stopping path remains executable from the current state. Transitioning to `Renewed` requires a strictly monotonic sequence counter, a newer parent belief record with an updated sensor capture epoch, and a fully passed admission re-check. A complex approach trajectory can span multiple consecutive lease renewals as long as fresh perception evidence continues to justify the motion. Dropping an isolated camera frame does not immediately abort tracking if the current coasting window remains valid. However, absent renewal, the hardware timer continues counting toward expiration. When an anomaly, force limit breach, or evidence timeout revokes tracking authority, the controller immediately engages a pre-calculated deceleration or hold trajectory to manage the kinetic energy of the moving manipulator safely.

@Fig-10-intent-lease-lifecycle draws the same machine. Its one subtle transition is the self-loop on a stale renewal. A packet with an old sequence number or an old capture is discarded without resetting the timer, so a host that keeps talking without new evidence still runs out of authority. Expiry and abort end in the same place, the validated fallback that the MCU selects for the measured state.

title: What the wheels allow
caption: **What the wheels allow**: (a) A differential-drive base with track width $\WheelTrackWidth$ can move forward at $\BaseForwardSpeed$ and turn at $\YawRate$ about the center of its axle, but its wheels cannot roll sideways. (b) A pure sideways offset is still reachable, as a maneuver rather than a step: turn in place, drive, and turn back. Proportions are schematic.
alt: Two top-view panels of a rectangular base with a drive wheel on each side. In the left panel, a solid arrow points forward along the heading, a curved arrow shows turning, a bracket marks the track width, and a dashed arrow pointing sideways is crossed out. In the right panel, a dashed sideways arrow between a start and a goal pose is crossed out, and a second path shows the base turned a quarter turn in place at the start, driving straight to the goal, and turning back, with the three steps numbered.
context:
The non-integrable relation in @eq-plan-unicycle forms a **nonholonomic constraint**\index{Nonholonomic constraint!differential drive},[^fn-holonomic-hertz-etymology] restricting the instantaneous velocity space without diminishing the dimension of the reachable configuration space $\PlanarSpecialEuclideanGroup$ [@siciliano2009robotics]. The base can reach any planar pose in the aisle, but not with any velocity. It can drive forward at $\BaseForwardSpeed$ and turn at $\YawRate$ about the center of its axle, while the no-slip condition forbids translation along the axle (@fig-11-nonholonomic-base). A pure sideways offset is therefore reached as a maneuver rather than a step: turn in place, drive along the new heading, and turn back. A base planner must therefore search directly over kinematically admissible control trajectories rather than straight geometric paths in configuration space. Furthermore, each wheel's tangential speed equals $\BaseForwardSpeed \pm \YawRate \WheelTrackWidth/2$ for track width $\WheelTrackWidth$, so hardware motor limits constrain linear velocity and turning rate jointly.

[^fn-holonomic-hertz-etymology]: **Holonomic** (Greek *holos*, whole, and *nomos*, law): @hertz1894prinzipien introduced the term for systems whose constraints obey integral laws, relations among positions alone, in contrast to material systems in general, which obey only differential laws. A wheel's no-slip rule is a differential law that cannot be integrated into such a relation. The distinction decides the planner's search space, since a holonomic arm can be planned as a path through configuration space while the base must be planned through its controls.\index{Holonomic constraint!etymology}

An independent protective safety scanner operates under its own hardware-to-actuation timing budget. When an obstacle breaches a safety-rated zone, the scanner's internal optical sampling, fail-safe output switching, safety controller logic, and drive disconnect delays entirely bypass the perception dispatch and software lease infrastructure. However, the physical response must still reserve the same underlying deceleration distance, mechanical tracking error, localization tolerance, and protective safety cushion; only computational delays bypassed by the safety bus are eliminated from the sum. Industrial mobile bases deploy such protective fields under ISO 3691-4 [@iso3691part4] for driverless industrial trucks and ISO 13849-1 [@iso13849part1] for safety-related control circuits, using a safety-rated planar scanner of the kind in @fig-12-real-laser-scanner, which evaluates programmable warning and protective fields. The physical dimensions of this protective field must be calculated from the dedicated scanner path's verified hardware timing budget, rather than inheriting the software lease and vision latencies of the neural planner. The safety-rated optical scanner is a component of a separately qualified protective function, distinct from the primary perception LiDAR that generates non-safety-rated point clouds for neural proposal generation. Its component rating does not certify the complete sensor-to-stop path. In the running architecture, that path must establish the detection coverage, response time, and physical stopping performance required for protection at rack intersections. @Sec-enforcement-certified-functions maps the software stopping budget onto this certified hardware baseline and shows that industrial vehicle testing standards validate pedestrian detection against the same static-obstacle assumption derived here.

context:
This geometric behavior exposes the distinction between **torque-space and task-space minimal intervention**\index{Minimal intervention!torque vs. task space}: an orthogonal projection $\CertifiedControlAction = \NominalControlCommand + \FiniteChange \ControlInput$ minimizes joint effort deviation $\|\ControlInput - \NominalControlCommand\|^2$, which redistributes multi-axis joint torques and rotates the net Cartesian wrench. While a feasible projection can preserve the safe set $\ForwardInvariantSafeSet$ under the stated model and timing assumptions, it deflects the end-effector trajectory and may arrest task progress. If the upstream neural policy continues emitting unprojected nominal setpoints without awareness of the intervention, the robot can chatter or stall at the boundary. The downstream enforcer must therefore stream the intervention vector $\FiniteChange \ControlInput$ back to the application processor as a telemetry signal, notifying the high-level planner to re-plan around the newly active physical constraint.

The same correction has a picture in state space and one in torque space (@fig-12-cbf-safety-filter). In state space, a trajectory that would breach the velocity-dependent boundary $\SafetyBoundaryManifold$ is turned along it; in the torque plane, the projection places $\CertifiedControlAction$ on the half-space boundary $\BarrierConstraintNormal^\top \ControlInput = \BarrierConstraintBound$, while the per-axis clamp leaves $\ClampedControlCommand$ outside it and skews its direction.

context:
1.  **Torque removal (Stage 3, drive side):** De-energizing the safety relays drops the drive's STO inputs, which de-energize the gate drive power supply for the three-phase inverter bridge, rendering the power MOSFETs or insulated-gate bipolar transistors (IGBTs) high-impedance, so the motor can no longer produce electromagnetic torque. STO alone does not apply mechanical braking. An unbraked motor carries momentum and may coast freely.
2.  **Mechanical restraint (Stage 3, brake side):** A separate coil circuit powers the spring-applied electromechanical friction brake. When power is removed, coil magnetic flux decays, allowing internal springs to physically clamp friction pads against the motor shaft, applying the brake without electrical power. A holding-brake rating does not establish the ability to arrest a moving load; dynamic stopping requires separate energy, torque, and response qualification.

context:
The pendant's red mushroom button is a different device with different semantics. Under ISO 13850, the emergency stop is a complementary protective measure, not a substitute for safeguarding or for the stop the risk assessment selects. It takes priority over every other function in every operating mode, it latches until an operator deliberately resets it at the device, and that reset must not restart the machine [@iso13850emergency]. Which physical response the stop invokes is a stop-category choice that @tbl-12-iec60204-stopping-categories maps to its evidence. The latch and the reset rule matter for supervisory control because they make a human stop sticky in exactly the way a network command is not. A remote packet can request a stop and a lease can lapse into one, but only the local reset of a latched device, followed by the fresh admission this chapter requires, returns the machine to motion.

[^fn-std-reduced-speed]: **Manual Reduced Speed**\index{Manual reduced speed!enabling devices}: ISO 10218-1:2025 limits the tool speed of an industrial robot in manual reduced-speed mode to $250\text{ mm/s}$ [@iso10218part1], the mode in which the pendant of @fig-14-teach-pendant couples motion to a three-position grip. Releasing or over-squeezing the grip only requests a stop from the safety circuit, and the performance level that circuit must reach, graded from PL a to PL e, is set by the machine's risk assessment under ISO 13849-1 [@iso13849part1]. The grip therefore bounds how fast the machine may be moving when a startled operator lets go, not which stop follows.

section: What each of the four rungs makes physical {#sec-verification-qualification-rungs}
context:
Two operational testing paradigms exist alongside this qualification ladder, but both break the closed loop entirely. Trace replay feeds recorded sensor streams into the candidate controller; while it preserves authentic sensor noise and optical artifacts, the recorded frames reflect the actions of the original historical policy rather than reacting to the candidate's new commands. Shadow operation runs the candidate model in parallel with an incumbent, validated controller. If the candidate proposes an aggressive velocity vector that would drive the base into a storage rack, the logger records the telemetry while the incumbent controller safely halts the base. Because neither approach permits candidate actions to alter future state observations, neither reveals the closed-loop physical consequences of an erroneous command.

A production shadow deployment cannot allow a stalled proposer to drive toward a human worker at a rack end to see if the brakes engage in time. A software simulator cannot expose a timing race between transceiver silicon buffers. An instrumented physical dynamometer cannot execute the tens of millions of randomized runs required to bound extreme distribution tails. Systems engineers must therefore route each fault injection scenario to the specific rung on the ladder that embodies its underlying physical and causal mechanism. In the running machine, `COND` selects a pre-validated safety configuration, much like industrial safety controllers and protective optical scanners switch between pre-validated field sets[^fn-scanner-field-sets] and speed-monitoring profiles. The workspace is discretized into a grid of vertical pillars, for example `{python} AppxBevFrustum.bev_cells_str` cells on a side covering a `{python} AppxBevFrustum.workspace_str` square at `{python} AppxBevFrustum.bev_res_str` resolution. The splat sums every frustum feature that falls within pillar $(\BevPillarXIndex, \BevPillarYIndex)$, using accelerated cumulative sums or point-pillar pooling [@philion2020lift; @liu2023bevfusion]:

Here $\CumulativeTransmittance_i$ represents cumulative optical transmittance along the viewing ray, initialized to $\CumulativeTransmittance_1=1$. In this rendering equation, $\PixelOpacityContribution_i$ is the pixel-dependent opacity contribution, including the projected Gaussian footprint, rather than the stored opacity $\GaussianPrimitiveOpacity_i$. An implementation may terminate when the remaining transmittance is sufficiently small; the error tolerance, scene density, and hardware determine the resulting speed.

However, a physical AI systems engineer must recognize the boundary between visual rendering and physical clearance. The 3D Gaussian parameters are optimized strictly against 2D photometric rendering loss (such as $\ell_1$ color difference and SSIM). Gaussians frequently fit unobserved scene regions with semi-transparent "floaters," hollow shells, or blurred volumetric density. Neither the stored opacity $\GaussianPrimitiveOpacity_i$ nor the spatial gradient $\nabla_{\CartesianPosition} \GaussianPrimitiveDensity_i(\CartesianPosition)$ of its density constitutes a conservative collision surface. @Fig-3dgs-slam-splatam partitions this architectural handoff across three functional panels. Panel (a) tracks camera poses from an incoming RGB-D stream. Panel (b) maintains the 3D Gaussian memory primitives (mean, covariance ellipsoid, opacity, and spherical-harmonic color) under adaptive splitting, cloning, and pruning. Panel (c) decouples photometric rasterization from physical safety, routing Gaussian primitives through an unvalidated candidate occupancy or signed distance field before an explicit error-bounding step admits the clearance envelope.

(b) Volumetric OctoMap voxel representation modeling 3D space as an 8-ary hierarchical tree, where occupied volumes are probabilistically updated and stored across variable resolutions. (c) Explicit free-space raycasting and lossless octree pruning, differentiating observed free cells (white voxels) from occupied obstacles (dark voxels) and unobserved unknown regions; free evidence alone does not certify traversability for a particular robot. #### Octree occupancy and free-space raycasting

Occupancy grid mapping [@elfes1989using] tessellates space into cells and applies this update to every cell a ray touches.\index{Occupancy grid mapping!octree storage} A volumetric raycast walks each return's sightline with the three-dimensional digital differential analyzer (3D-DDA) traversal [@amanatides1987fast].\index{Volumetric free-space raycasting!3D-DDA traversal} Hierarchical stores such as OctoMap [@hornung2013octomap] and OpenVDB [@museth2013vdb] allocate cells only where rays have passed, so storage follows the observed volume rather than the bounding cube. @Fig-09-octomap-volumetric-mapping traces this spatial-memory pipeline across three successive representations during an indoor mobile robot traversal. ## The Intersection Landscape {#sec-appendix-spa-intersections}

When a mobile manipulator clips a cart that just rolled out of a cross-aisle, the fault often spans more than one subsystem: a voxel layer that held a stale free-space timestamp, a trajectory handoff that delayed braking, or a shared memory bus that stalled the safety check. @Fig-spa-triad diagrams the Sense, Plan, and Act (S·P·A) triad as three intersecting functional domains. Its three pairwise interfaces are $\Glyph{S} \cap \Glyph{P}$ (locating object position in current time), $\Glyph{P} \cap \Glyph{A}$ (verifying that proposed trajectories satisfy dynamic limits), and $\Glyph{A} \cap \Glyph{S}$ (measuring physical state evolution after actuation). The independent permission decision sits at their central three-way intersection ($\Glyph{S} \cap \Glyph{P} \cap \Glyph{A}$), where a qualified permission path gates all motor commands against physical budgets before actuation. Each intersection below pairs its physical handoff contract with a discriminating measurement.
